The East India Company (EIC) was incorporated by royal charter on December 31, 1600, when Queen Elizabeth I granted a charter to a group of London merchants for exclusive overseas trading rights with the East Indies [d2][d3][d6]. It was an English joint-stock company originally formed for the exploitation of trade with East and Southeast Asia and India [d2][d7]. According to one source, the merchants had already organized in 1599 before the formal charter was granted in 1600 [d9], and the company was founded during the rule of Queen Elizabeth I, who created a monopoly on English trade to the East Indies [d5]. Formed in 1600, the EIC traded in Asian textiles, spices, porcelain, and tea, eventually growing into a powerful commercial and political organization [d8][d7], and was ultimately dissolved in 1874 [d1][d4].
